newsitem.title: PERU: Peru strikes law that allowed marriage after rape.
newsitem.headline: Peru strikes law that allowed marriage after rape.

text.p: The Peruvian Congress, heeding calls by feminists worldwide, voted overwhelmingly on Thursday to repeal a law dating from 1924 that allows rapists to go free if they marry their victims.
The bill, strongly supported by women's groups, passed by a vote of 86 to 1, though most of the bill's opponents left the hall before the vote.

The long-awaited vote will abolish a law which allows rapists to escape all criminal prosecution if they persuade -- or threaten -- their victim into marrying them. The law also allows all perpetrators of a gang rape to go free if only one of them marries the victim.
The debate attracted international attention, particularly since at least 15 other countries in Latin America have similar laws, which may now come under more scrutiny.
"This is a great victory for Peruvian women and also for Peruvian men since all of us together can celebrate the end of this embarrassment," said congresswoman Beatriz Merino, who sponsored the bill.
"We are eliminating a juridical aberration, an archaic law that has been in effect since the beginning of the century," she told reporters.

Supporters said they were confident President Alberto Fujimori would sign the repeal into law. Fujimori has made women's rights a feature of his government and was the only male head-of-state to speak at the U.N. women's conference in Beijing in 1995.
Opponents of repeal had said the law as it stands favours the development of families and that women were free to refuse marriage and file charges against the rapist if they wanted to.

"The text (of the bill) damages the dignity of the Peruvian woman," said Xavier Barron of the centre-right Popular Christian Party, the sole member of Congress to vote against repeal. "I don't think there should be a pardon of any kind for rapists," he told Reuters.
Women's groups say scores of Peruvian men take advantage of the law every year to escape prosecution for rape, particularly in poor and rural areas.

Merino said the repeal puts Peru "in the vanguard" of efforts in Latin America to strike archaic and repressive rape laws from the books. The region's growing feminist movement has faced an uphill struggle in countries where the concept of machismo was born.
